```{r setup}
library(ffp)
```

## What diagnostics are for

An Entropy Pooling model translates economic or statistical views into
constraints on posterior scenario probabilities. Once the model is fitted,
there are therefore two different questions to ask.

The first is numerical: did the posterior probabilities satisfy the
constraints that define the model? The second is economic: how did satisfying
those constraints change the distribution?

`ffp_diagnostics()` is designed for the first question. It connects the
user-facing views to the mathematical constraints compiled by `ffp` and
evaluates whether those constraints are satisfied by the fitted posterior.

Distributional functions such as `ffp_stats()`, `ffp_risk()`, and
`ffp_moments()` answer the second question. They describe the consequences of
the posterior rather than the numerical quality of the fit.

<!-- > **Diagnostics tell us whether the posterior solves the model we specified. -->
<!-- > Statistics and risk measures tell us what that posterior means.** -->

This distinction is especially useful because a view is not necessarily one
mathematical constraint. A mean view produces one equality, whereas a quantile
view generates two inequalities. Diagnostics allow us to move between these
two levels without requiring users to work directly with constraint matrices.

## A regular Entropy Pooling model

We begin with a small scenario set so that the relationship between views and
constraints remains transparent.

```{r scenarios}
scenarios <- tibble::tibble(
  equity = c(-0.08, -0.03, 0.00, 0.04, 0.08)
)
scenarios
```

We assign a uniform prior and impose two views. The first raises the expected
equity return to 2%. The second requires \(-3\%\) to belong to the set of
posterior 20% quantiles.

```{r regular-model}
model <- scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = 0.02),
    view_quantile(equity, target = -0.03, level = 0.20)
  )

model
```

The full-confidence Entropy Pooling problem reads:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_p
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\log\left(
\frac{p_t}{q_t}
\right)
\\[4pt]
\text{subject to}
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t x_t
=
0.02,
\\
&\quad
P_p(X < -0.03)
\leq
0.20,
\\
&\quad
P_p(X > -0.03)
\leq
0.80,
\\
&\quad
p_t \geq 0,
\\
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T} p_t = 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The model contains two semantic views but three mathematical constraints:
one equality from `view_mean()` and two inequalities from
`view_quantile()`.

We can now fit the model:

```{r regular-fit}
fit <- ffp_fit(model)
fit
```

A successful `<ffp_fit>` contains the posterior probabilities together with
the prior, compiled constraints, solver result and original model. This makes
it possible to diagnose the fitted model without reconstructing any of the
original view information.

## Start with the fit print

Printing a fitted model provides a first numerical screening.

The output contains the number of scenarios, number of semantic views, the solver
status, the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between posterior and prior, and the maximum
numerical residual.

The KL divergence is:

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \Vert q)
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\log\left(
\frac{p_t}{q_t}
\right).
$$

It measures how far the posterior probability distribution moved from the
prior in relative-entropy terms. A larger KL divergence means that more
probability distortion was required to satisfy the views, but it should not be
interpreted as a generic goodness-of-fit statistic.

The reported `Max residual` has a different purpose. It is the largest among
the probability-normalization residual, the largest equality residual, and
the largest inequality violation. It therefore summarizes numerical
constraint satisfaction rather than the economic importance of the posterior
update.

The solver `Status` should also be interpreted narrowly. A successful
optimization normally reports `converged`; when the prior already satisfies
all constraints, the fit can instead report `prior_satisfies_constraints`.
These are solver outcomes, not measures of how economically important the
views are.

## A compact summary

`summary()` adds another useful layer without exposing every mathematical
constraint.

```{r fit-summary}
summary(fit)
```

In addition to the information shown by `print(fit)`, the summary reports how
many semantic views are satisfied, how many inequality constraints were
compiled, and how many of those inequalities are numerically binding.

This is often enough for a routine check. If all views are satisfied and the
maximum residual is small relative to the tolerance used for fitting, the user
can usually proceed to interpreting the posterior distribution.

When more detail is needed, `ffp_diagnostics()` provides the mapping from views
to their underlying constraints.

## Diagnose the views

By default, `ffp_diagnostics()` works at the same semantic level used to
specify the model:

```{r view-diagnostics}
view_diagnostics <- ffp_diagnostics(fit)
view_diagnostics
```

Each row corresponds to one view added through `ffp_view()`. The output reports
the view method and expression together with the number of mathematical
constraints generated by that view.

For each semantic view, `max_error` is the largest equality residual or
inequality violation generated by its constraints. The `status` is
`satisfied` when every underlying constraint is satisfied within the numerical
tolerance stored in the fit.

This level is intended to answer a simple question: did the posterior satisfy 
each view that I specified?

In our example, the mean view corresponds to one equality, while the quantile
view corresponds to two inequalities. The default diagnostic output preserves
this distinction without requiring the user to inspect the constraint matrices
directly.

## Inspect the mathematical constraints

Advanced diagnostics are available by requesting the constraint level.

```{r constraint-diagnostics}
constraint_diagnostics <- ffp_diagnostics(fit, level = "constraint")
constraint_diagnostics
```

The output now contains one row for each compiled mathematical constraint.
Besides metadata connecting each constraint to its semantic view, the table
reports `lhs`, `rhs`, `gap`, and the diagnostic quantities appropriate for
equalities and inequalities.

This level is useful when a view expands into several constraints, when an
inequality is close to binding, or when the user wants to inspect the exact
linear representation solved by Entropy Pooling.

It is important to remember that `lhs` and `rhs` refer to the **compiled
constraint**. For views such as conditional probabilities, volatility,
covariance, and correlation, the user-facing statement is transformed into an
equivalent linear expression before optimization. The diagnostic values
therefore need not look numerically identical to the original target supplied
to the view constructor.

## Equality constraints

An equality constraint has the generic form

$$
a'p = b.
$$

For equalities, diagnostics report

$$
\text{gap}
=
a'p-b
$$

and

$$
\text{residual}
=
|a'p-b|.
$$

We can isolate the equality generated by our mean view.

```{r equality-diagnostics}
constraint_diagnostics |>
  dplyr::filter(constraint_type == "equality") |>
  dplyr::select(view_id, constraint:residual, satisfied)
```

The theoretical target is exact, but a numerical optimizer operates with
finite precision. A residual such as \(10^{-10}\) or \(10^{-12}\) therefore
does not mean that the model imposed only partial confidence in the view. It
means that the numerical solution differs from the exact equality by that
small amount.

Equality constraints do not have a meaningful `binding` status in
`ffp_diagnostics()`. They are either satisfied within tolerance or they are
not, so `binding` is reported as `NA` for equalities.

## Inequality constraints

Inequalities are represented internally in the form

$$
a'p \leq b.
$$

Their diagnostics require a slightly different interpretation. The gap remains

$$
\text{gap}
=
a'p-b,
$$

but the slack is

$$
\text{slack}
=
b-a'p.
$$

The numerical violation is

$$
\text{violation}
=
\max(a'p-b,0).
$$

The two inequalities generated by our quantile view can be inspected directly.

```{r inequality-diagnostics}
constraint_diagnostics |>
  dplyr::filter(constraint_type == "inequality") |>
  dplyr::select(view_id, constraint:residual, satisfied)
```

A positive slack is not a problem. It means that the inequality is satisfied
with room to spare. An inequality becomes numerically binding when the absolute
slack is sufficiently close to zero under the `constraint_tolerance` stored in
the fitted model.

This distinction is particularly useful for quantile and ranking views. A
quantile target produces two inequalities, but the posterior does not need to
make both of them binding. One side may determine the solution while the other
remains satisfied with positive slack.

## Numerical tolerance

Entropy Pooling views describe mathematical properties of the posterior, but
those properties must ultimately be verified numerically.

The tolerance used by the fitted model is stored with the solver result.

```{r stored-tolerance}
fit$solver$control$constraint_tolerance
```

`ffp_diagnostics()` uses this stored value rather than the current package
default. The diagnostic interpretation of a fitted object therefore remains
consistent with the numerical settings under which that object was created.

For example, an inequality with a very small positive slack may be classified
as binding under a looser tolerance but non-binding under a stricter one. The
underlying posterior and economic view have not changed; only the numerical
definition of "close enough to the boundary" differs.

Advanced users can change the numerical controls when fitting:

```{r solver-control, eval = FALSE}
control <- entropy_solver_control(constraint_tolerance = 1e-9)

fit <- ffp_fit(model, control = control)
```

<!-- The important distinction is conceptual: -->

<!-- > **View confidence is a modeling choice. Solver tolerance is a numerical -->
<!-- > choice. They are not the same thing.** -->

`ffp_fit()` imposes views with full confidence. Partial confidence is introduced
separately with `ffp_opinion_pooling()` rather than by loosening solver
tolerances.

## Regular, boundary, and infeasible problems

Constraint diagnostics apply to a successfully fitted `<ffp_fit>` object.
However, some combinations of scenario support, prior probabilities and views
cannot be represented by the regular dual Entropy Pooling solution.

It is useful to distinguish three broad cases:

| Case | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Regular | A feasible solution exists in the relevant interior of the prior support |
| Boundary | A feasible solution exists, but it requires probabilities on a boundary that the current dual solver cannot attain exactly |
| Infeasible | No probability distribution can satisfy all constraints simultaneously |

The distinction between boundary and infeasible is fundamental. A boundary
problem has a mathematically valid probability solution. An infeasible problem
does not.

The current solver identifies these situations while fitting and raises a
specific error rather than returning an invalid or misleading `<ffp_fit>`.

### A regular solution

Our first example is regular. The desired mean and quantile can be achieved
without forcing a positive-prior scenario to have exactly zero probability.

The dual optimizer therefore returns a valid posterior and
`ffp_diagnostics()` can subsequently evaluate its view and constraint
satisfaction.

Regular should not be interpreted as "small posterior change." A regular
problem can still produce a substantial KL divergence or a concentrated
posterior. The classification concerns the geometry and feasibility of the
constraint problem, not the economic magnitude of the update.

## Boundary solutions

A simple way to understand a boundary problem is to consider a mean view at
the extreme of the scenario support.

The largest equity return in our scenario set is

```{r support-maximum}
max(scenarios$equity)
```

Now suppose the full-confidence view requires the posterior expected return to
equal this maximum.

```{r boundary-model}
boundary_model <- scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = max(scenarios$equity))
  )
```

For any probability distribution over these scenarios,

$$
E_p[X]
\leq
\max_t X_t.
$$

Equality can hold only if all posterior probability is assigned to scenarios
at the maximum. Every lower-return scenario must therefore receive zero
posterior probability.

The optimization problem is mathematically feasible, but its solution lies on
a face of the probability simplex. Because the uniform prior assigns positive
probability to every scenario, the current dual solver cannot attain this
solution exactly while maintaining its positive-probability representation.

`ffp_fit()` detects this geometry and reports it explicitly.

```{r boundary-fit, error = TRUE}
ffp_fit(boundary_model)
```

The important interpretation is: the view is feasible, but satisfying it 
exactly requires a boundary posterior.

This is different from numerical non-convergence and different from an
infeasible economic view. Changing optimizer iterations or arbitrarily relaxing
tolerances is therefore not the natural first response. The user should first
consider whether an exact full-confidence corner solution is really the
intended model.

### Prior-support boundaries

A second kind of boundary arises when the prior assigns exactly zero
probability to a scenario but a view would require that scenario to receive
positive posterior probability.

Consider:

```{r prior-support-model}
support_scenarios <- tibble::tibble(
  event = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
)

support_model <- support_scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_custom(c(0, 0.50, 0.50))
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_probability(event, target = 0.20)
  )
```

The only scenario in which `event` is true has zero prior probability. The view
therefore requires positive posterior probability at a point outside the
positive support of the prior.

```{r prior-support-fit, error = TRUE}
ffp_fit(support_model)
```

This problem is feasible if we consider the scenario set alone, but it is not
feasible within the support of the current prior. Under KL-based Entropy
Pooling, a zero prior probability is therefore a substantive modeling choice,
not merely a very small weight.

## Infeasible views

An infeasible problem is different because no probability distribution on the
available scenarios can satisfy the views.

Suppose we require an expected equity return above the maximum available
scenario:

```{r infeasible-model}
infeasible_model <- scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = 0.10)
  )
```

Every probability-weighted mean over a fixed one-dimensional support must
satisfy:

$$
\min_t X_t
\leq
E_p[X]
\leq
\max_t X_t.
$$

Our scenarios have a maximum equity return of 8%, so a full-confidence target
of 10% cannot be obtained by any non-negative probability vector summing to
one.

`ffp_fit()` therefore identifies the Entropy Pooling problem as infeasible:

```{r infeasible-fit, error = TRUE}
ffp_fit(infeasible_model)
```

No `<ffp_fit>` object exists in this case, so there is nothing to pass to
`ffp_diagnostics()`. The appropriate response is to revisit the model itself:
the view may be impossible, several views may be mutually contradictory, or
the scenario support may not contain the states required by the intended
analysis.

Before changing solver settings, ask whether the requested posterior can 
exist on the available scenario support. This is especially important for 
extreme views. Entropy Pooling can reweight available scenarios, but it 
cannot create an economically relevant state that is absent from the 
scenario set.

## Numerical failure is different again

A regular mathematical problem can still encounter a numerical optimization
failure. This is conceptually different from both boundary and infeasible
problems.

The current solver examines the constraint problem when ordinary optimization
does not produce a valid solution. If the mathematical problem is classified
as regular, a failure is treated as numerical rather than being mislabeled as
economic infeasibility.

This distinction matters when deciding what to change. An infeasible problem
requires revisiting views or scenario support. A boundary problem requires
recognizing that the exact solution lies outside the interior representation of
the current solver. A genuinely numerical problem may justify examining
solver controls, scaling, redundant constraints, or conditioning.

Most users should nevertheless begin with the default solver settings, which
are intended for typical applications.

## Diagnostics are not economic interpretation

Once a fit has passed its numerical checks, diagnostics have largely completed
their task. A residual close to zero tells us that a view was satisfied; it
does not tell us whether satisfying the view changed the posterior distribution
in an economically meaningful way.

Similarly, an inequality being binding tells us something about the geometry
of the fitted constraint set, but not whether portfolio risk rose or fell.
KL divergence measures probability distortion, but it is not by itself a
measure of investment relevance.

Economic interpretation belongs to the post-fit distribution tools.

```{r economic-interpretation}
ffp_stats(fit)

ffp_risk(fit, confidence = 0.99)
```

Visual comparison of prior and posterior distributions can provide another
perspective.

```{r diagnostic-plot, eval = FALSE}
autoplot(fit)
```

The Effective Number of Scenarios reported through distributional summaries
also belongs on this side of the analysis. ENS measures concentration of
probability mass rather than numerical satisfaction of the Entropy Pooling
constraints.

## A practical diagnostic workflow

For most fitted models, a diagnostic review can remain simple. Begin with the
printed `<ffp_fit>` and `summary(fit)` to check solver status, KL divergence,
maximum residual, satisfied views, and binding inequalities. Then use
`ffp_diagnostics(fit)` to verify each semantic view. Constraint-level
diagnostics are most useful when a view expands into several mathematical
conditions or when an inequality is close to binding.

Only after those numerical questions are understood should the analysis move
to `ffp_stats()`, `ffp_risk()`, `ffp_moments()`, or visualization to determine
what the posterior means economically.

If `ffp_fit()` instead reports a boundary or infeasible problem, there is no
fitted posterior to diagnose. In that case, the error itself is part of the
diagnostic workflow: it identifies whether the requested solution exists only
on a problematic boundary or cannot exist at all on the available support.

This separation keeps three different questions distinct: whether the model is
mathematically feasible, whether the numerical solution satisfies the model,
and what the resulting posterior distribution means for the application.

## Where to go next

The three main layers of the `ffp` workflow now answer complementary questions.

The model and view interface defines the scenario support, prior information,
and statements that should hold under the posterior. `ffp_fit()` and
`ffp_diagnostics()` determine whether those statements form a feasible
full-confidence Entropy Pooling problem and whether the resulting probabilities
satisfy its constraints numerically. Finally, the distributional tools describe
how that posterior changes moments, tail risk, scenario concentration, and
other economically relevant quantities.

When the views themselves are uncertain, `ffp_opinion_pooling()` adds a
separate modeling layer for confidence without changing the numerical meaning
of the original full-confidence fit.

Together, these components separate **model specification**, **numerical
validation**, **view confidence**, and **economic interpretation**. This
separation is intended to make Entropy Pooling models easier to understand,
diagnose, and use in downstream decisions.
